title: Thread Pools and Work Stealing
description: Little's Law for pool sizing, Java ForkJoinPool, work stealing algorithm, backpressure with bounded queues, and Java 21 virtual threads (Project Loom).

segments.text: Thread pools are the workhorse of concurrent systems. Every web server, every database connection handler, and every background job processor uses one. Getting the pool size right determines whether your system handles load gracefully or collapses. This lesson covers the math and the mechanisms.

Little's Law: L equals lambda times W. The number of tasks in the system equals the arrival rate times the average processing time. If requests arrive at 1,000 per second and each takes 50 milliseconds, you need 50 concurrent workers. This gives you a mathematical lower bound for pool size. Below this, requests queue; above this, you waste resources.

For CPU-bound tasks, optimal pool size equals the number of CPU cores. More threads cause context switching without improving throughput. For I/O-bound tasks, pool size equals cores times the ratio of wait time to compute time. If a task waits 90 percent of the time on I/O, pool size is cores times 10. A 4-core server can handle 40 I/O-bound threads effectively.

A fixed-size thread pool maintains a constant number of workers. Tasks go into a queue. Workers pull tasks when available. Java's FixedThreadPool uses an unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue. This is dangerous: if tasks arrive faster than they're processed, the queue grows without limit, consuming memory until OOM. Always use bounded queues in production.

When a bounded queue fills up, you need a rejection policy. AbortPolicy throws an exception — fail fast. CallerRunsPolicy makes the submitting thread execute the task itself — natural backpressure that slows the producer. DiscardPolicy silently drops the task. DiscardOldestPolicy drops the oldest queued task. CallerRunsPolicy is usually the best default for web servers.
segments.thought_prompt: Why is CallerRunsPolicy natural backpressure? What happens to the request accept rate when it kicks in?

segments.text: Java's ForkJoinPool is designed for divide-and-conquer parallelism. Split a large task into subtasks, process in parallel, merge results. Each worker thread has its own deque. When a worker finishes its tasks, it steals from the tail of another worker's deque. This is work stealing — it maximizes CPU utilization without a centralized task queue bottleneck.

Work stealing's elegance is in the deque. A worker pushes and pops from the top of its own deque — LIFO for cache locality. Thieves steal from the bottom — FIFO for large tasks. The deque is lock-free for the owning thread and uses CAS for stealing. Contention only occurs when a deque is nearly empty. Tokio, Go's runtime, and Java's ForkJoinPool all use this algorithm.

Go's runtime uses M:N scheduling. Goroutines, lightweight green threads, are multiplexed onto OS threads. The runtime uses work-stealing across processor-local queues. A goroutine costs only 2 to 8 kilobytes of stack, growing as needed. You can run millions of goroutines without the overhead of OS threads. This is why Go handles massive concurrency so naturally.

Java 21's virtual threads, from Project Loom, bring the same M:N model to Java. A virtual thread is a lightweight thread managed by the JVM, not the OS. Creating a million virtual threads takes seconds and megabytes. When a virtual thread blocks on I/O, the carrier OS thread is freed to run other virtual threads. This eliminates the need for reactive programming in many cases.

Virtual threads have gotchas. Synchronized blocks pin the virtual thread to its carrier OS thread, preventing other virtual threads from using it. Use ReentrantLock instead. Thread-local variables are expensive with millions of threads — use scoped values instead. And virtual threads don't help CPU-bound work; they're designed for I/O-bound concurrency.

Your service processes image uploads. Each upload takes 100 milliseconds of CPU work for resizing plus 200 milliseconds of I/O for storage. You have 8 CPU cores and receive 500 uploads per second. How would you design the thread pool architecture? Would you use one pool or separate pools for CPU and I/O work?
segments.thought_prompt: Should CPU-bound and I/O-bound work share a thread pool, or should they be separated? Calculate the sizes.

segments.text: Thread pool sizing isn't guesswork — use Little's Law. Always use bounded queues with explicit rejection policies. Work stealing maximizes utilization without centralized bottlenecks. Virtual threads in Java 21 and goroutines in Go eliminate the thread-per-request scaling limit. The future is lightweight threads, but the fundamentals of pool sizing and backpressure still apply.
